summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) but fuel price pressures remain high and actual fuel savings are far below the theoretical ceiling. Public transport ridership is recovering yet still 10% below the 2025 benchmark, while high‑risk sectors show limited work‑from‑home adoption, raising economic and equity concerns.

signals.detail: Only 334,000 litres were saved in the first week of the mandate, less than 1% of the modelled ceiling of 35.7 M L/week, indicating a large compliance gap despite a 100/100 fuel policy component.
Daily PT trips total 1,235,713, projecting to about 451 M trips annually—roughly 10% below the 2025 recovery level of 506 M, showing a modest rebound but still short of pre‑pandemic demand.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction exhibit mobility scores above 85 with WFH rates under 15%, exposing these sectors to fuel price volatility and congestion risks as the economy normalises.
WFH adoption is uneven—public & GLCs at 60% versus Construction at 5%—creating disparate exposure to commuting costs and limiting the fairness of the current mandate.

High fuel prices (RON95 RM 4.42/L) and a perfect fuel‑policy score suggest price‑driven incentives for modal shift, yet the MF‑Index remains near‑normal and PT ridership has not fully capitalised on this pressure.

recommendation: Introduce targeted WFH incentives for Logistics, Retail & Services, and Construction to raise sectoral WFH rates to at least 30% by Q2 2027, coupled with a graduated fuel‑tax rebate for commuters who shift to public transport. Aim to lift daily PT trips to 1.35 M (≈480 M annually) and achieve a minimum 5% real fuel‑saving benchmark within the next six months.
